newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Ford to crank-start world's largest magnesium plant.
newsitem.headline: Ford to crank-start world's largest magnesium plant.

text.p: U.S. auto giant Ford Motor Co on Thursday unveiled a partnership with Australia's Queensland Metals Corp (QMC) to secure supply of a metal that is changing the face of automotive design.

"This new Australian project could well revolutionise our approach to the use of magnesium in automotive manufacturing around the world," Ford Australia's president David Morgan told a news conference.

Ford, through its Australian unit, has agreed to pump nearly A$40 million ($31 million) into a pilot smelter in Queensland state which, if successful, will be expanded to a 90,000 tonne commercial facility at a cost of A$700 million.

"We intend to develop a demonstration plant ... conduct a feasibility study on a commercial smelter and move in 1999 to construction of the world's largest magnesium production facility," QMC chairman Ian Howard-Smith told reporters.

While Ford would not be investing in the full-scale smelter, it said it had contracted to take up to half its annual output for 10 years -- a deal worth roughly A$1.5 billion -- from the time the plant reaches designed capacity in 2004.
"The partnership effectively guarantees the automotive company a long-term stable supply of high-grade, low-cost material," Morgan said.
Ford is keen to build cars using a higher proportion of magnesium, which it says is four times lighter than steel and half the weight of aluminium while being stronger and more ductile than both.
"Ford anticipates its future use of the metal will more than treble as a result of the agreement," Morgan said.

"What you're seeing is a greater push toward greater fuel economy and lower emissions and one of the ways to achieve that is lower vehicle weight. The advantage of using magnesium alloys in that is to give us a lower-weight vehicle."
Ford cars typically contain about one kilogram (2.2 pounds) of magnesium alloys and the company is currently the world's largest consumer of magnesium.
But in the past, the automotive giant has had to buy the metal from geographically scattered sources which it said offered variable quality.
"At the moment, we mainly get it from China and Russia," Morgan said.

By comparison, the QMC plant, which would initially be owned by an equal joint venture with Normandy Mining Ltd, would churn out consistently high-quality ingots using top-grade ore from the giant Kunwarara deposit in Queensland, Ford said.

The plant also would use a low-cost process developed over the past 10 years by QMC and the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), an Australian government-funded think-tank.
"This project represents a commitment to a major new industry in Australian and is capable of transforming QMC into a world-scale producer of low-cost magnesium metal," QMC said in a statement.
Ford is not the first player in the automotive industry to make upstream investments to secure the supply of magnesium for its future fleet.
Last year, Germany's Volkswagen AG entered a joint venture to build a plant that would eventually extract 27,000 tonnes of magnesium a year from the Dead Sea.
One-third of that plant's output has been earmarked for VW to use in producing auto parts.
